neighbors.heading: a leaf, a flower
neighbors.text: Today a coin a week, from many small hands, crossed an ocean, and Jesus praised a widow's two tiny coins. Hindus hear a promise like that in the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna says that whoever offers him, with love, a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water, he accepts it, because it was given from a loving heart.
neighbors.difference: In Mark's Gospel, the widow gives to the temple treasury, and Pauline's coins fed missions far away. In the Gita, the small gift is offered to Krishna himself, often at a home shrine, and many Hindus then share it as prasad, blessed food.
neighbors.shared: the size of the gift was never the point.

neighbors.heading: an atom's weight
neighbors.text: Today a coin a week, from many hands, crossed an ocean, and Jesus praised a widow's two tiny coins. The Qur'an makes room for the smallest good too: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then." And the Prophet Muhammad told his companions to shield themselves from the Fire, even with half a date given away.
neighbors.difference: Pauline's circles gave freely, by choice, for the missions. In Islam, beside free gifts called sadaqa, there is zakat: a set share of wealth given each year to those in need, one of the five pillars.
neighbors.shared: no gift is too small to count.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 99:7 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Zakat, the hadith of half a date (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the gospel at the factory gate
neighbors.text: Today a pope wrote that a worker is a person, never a tool, and is owed a fair wage. Protestant Christians were wrestling with the same factories. Walter Rauschenbusch, a Baptist pastor in a poor New York neighborhood, watched his people worn down by work and poverty, and argued that the gospel speaks to wages, hours and housing, not only to the soul.
neighbors.difference: Rerum Novarum is a teaching letter from the pope to the whole Church. The Social Gospel was a movement of many Protestant pastors and writers, with no single voice speaking for every church.
neighbors.shared: work is done by people, and people deserve dignity.
neighbors.sources: Walter Rauschenbusch, Christianity and the Social Crisis (1907) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: bread from honest hands
neighbors.text: Today a pope said a worker is a person, never a tool. Sikhs tell a story about Guru Nanak. Invited to a rich official's feast, he ate instead with Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter. In the story, he squeezed Lalo's plain bread and milk flowed; he squeezed the rich man's bread and blood dripped out, wrung from the poor.
neighbors.difference: Rerum Novarum argues for just wages and the right to form unions. Sikh teaching makes honest work, kirat karni, one of three daily pillars, beside remembering God's Name and sharing what you earn.
neighbors.shared: honest work, and fair pay for it, is holy ground.
neighbors.sources: Janamsakhi tradition, Guru Nanak and Bhai Lalo (paraphrase) · Sikh teaching of naam japna, kirat karni, vand chhakna (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one father
neighbors.text: Today Charles de Foucauld lived among the Tuareg as a brother to anyone at his door. A Hebrew prophet asked the question his life answered: "Have we not all one father? Hath not one God created us?" Malachi asks it of his own people, who were quarreling with each other, and many readers hear it reaching every human being.
neighbors.difference: Foucauld saw every person as his brother through Jesus, the one master of Matthew's Gospel. In Malachi, the bond runs straight to the one Creator, with no one between, and the prophet calls his own community back to keep faith with each other.
neighbors.shared: the stranger at the door is family you haven't met yet.

neighbors.heading: a boundless heart
neighbors.text: Today Charles de Foucauld wanted to be a brother to everyone who knocked at his door. Buddhists practice that wide heart on purpose. The Metta Sutta asks for kindness without limits: as a mother would guard her only child with her life, so toward all living beings, near or far, seen or unseen, let your heart be boundless.
neighbors.difference: For Foucauld, everyone is a brother because God is the one Father of all. The Metta Sutta names no creator; kindness is a training of the mind, offered to every living being, animals and unseen beings included.
neighbors.shared: no one is outside the circle of your kindness.

neighbors.heading: tie your camel, and trust
neighbors.text: Today Padre Pio left three words: pray, hope, don't worry. Muslims call that kind of trust tawakkul. The Qur'an says that whoever puts their trust in God, he is enough for them. And when a man asked the Prophet Muhammad whether to tie his camel or simply trust God, the answer was: tie it, and trust.
neighbors.difference: Padre Pio trusted God made known in Christ, whose wounds he was believed to carry in his own body. In Islam, trust goes to God alone, and the Prophet is a messenger who shows the way.
neighbors.shared: do your part, then let your heart rest.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 65:3 (paraphrase) · Jami' at-Tirmidhi, the hadith of the camel (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: what's up to you
neighbors.text: Today Padre Pio said: pray, hope, don't worry. Long before him, a Greek teacher who had once been a slave, Epictetus, opened his handbook the same way: some things are up to us, and some are not. Our choices and efforts are ours; much else is not. Worry, he taught, comes from gripping what was never ours to hold.
neighbors.difference: Padre Pio's calm leaned on a God who hears prayer and cares for each person. Epictetus grounds it mainly in clear thinking: sort what is yours from what isn't, and peace follows from the sorting.
neighbors.shared: you can set down what was never yours to carry.

neighbors.heading: the kitchen with an open door
neighbors.text: Today Dorothy Day opened a door, and hungry people came in for soup and coffee. Sikhs keep a door like that at the gurdwara: the langar, a free kitchen that tradition traces to Guru Nanak. Anyone may eat, of any faith or none. Everyone sits together on the floor, in rows, rich beside poor, and volunteers cook and serve.
neighbors.difference: Dorothy Day's houses grew from the Gospel and Catholic teaching on the poor, run by a movement of volunteers. For Sikhs, langar is part of the gurdwara itself, and sitting side by side on the floor teaches that no caste or rank sets anyone apart.
neighbors.shared: the hungry stranger at the door gets a seat and a plate.

neighbors.heading: the guest as god
neighbors.text: Today Dorothy Day opened her house, and whoever came hungry was fed. An old Hindu teaching treats the guest that way. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends students home with parting words: honor your mother as a god, your father, your teacher, and your guest as a god too. The phrase is still widely quoted: atithi devo bhava.
neighbors.difference: Dorothy Day saw Christ himself in the hungry at her door, as Jesus taught in Matthew's Gospel. For many Hindus, the guest is honored as a god, or as God arriving unannounced, and the welcome is a household duty and a sacred one.
neighbors.shared: whoever knocks hungry is a guest worth honoring.

neighbors.heading: hatred doesn't end hatred
neighbors.text: Today Polish workers faced a hard government with strikes, prayer and no violence, and Paul's line: overcome evil by good. Buddhists keep a verse near the start of the Dhammapada: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." The Buddha speaks of it as the way things work, in every age.
neighbors.difference: Paul's line rests on God, who judges and will set things right, so Christians need not repay evil. The Dhammapada speaks of cause and effect in the heart: answering hate with hate only feeds it, and whoever lets it go is freed.
neighbors.shared: the way out of hate is never more hate.

neighbors.heading: love your enemies, out loud
neighbors.text: Today Polish workers took on a hard government without violence. American Christians did something like it. Martin Luther King Jr., a Baptist preacher, led marches for civil rights rooted in Jesus' words: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you." He preached that hate cannot drive out hate; only love can do that.
neighbors.difference: Solidarity was a trade union, backed by a pope, with strikers kneeling at Mass in the shipyard. The civil rights movement grew largely from Black churches, many of them Baptist, led by preachers from their own congregations.
neighbors.shared: you can stand up and still refuse to hate.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 5:44 (KJV) · Martin Luther King Jr., Strength to Love (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: they don't see the good
neighbors.text: Today a pope sat in a prison cell beside the man who shot him. A Roman emperor, Marcus Aurelius, began his days by expecting the rude and the ungrateful, and reminding himself: they do wrong because they don't see what's good. And we're made to work together, he wrote, like two hands, so he would not stay angry with his own kin.
neighbors.difference: John Paul forgave as a Christian, following Jesus, and called the gunman his brother before God. Marcus works it out by reason: people act from not knowing better, and nursing anger goes against our nature as people made for each other.
neighbors.shared: you can name the wrong and still not carry the anger.

neighbors.heading: don't be cruel
neighbors.text: Today a pope forgave the man who shot him, then went to sit with him. Judaism teaches forgiving too. Maimonides wrote that when someone who wronged you asks forgiveness, you shouldn't be cruel and refuse; forgive with a whole heart. And before Yom Kippur, Jews are taught to go to the people they've hurt, because the day itself atones only for wrongs against God.
neighbors.difference: John Paul forgave publicly before he was asked. In Jewish teaching, the person who did the harm is expected to come, ask, and make it right, and forgiveness is owed once they sincerely do.
neighbors.shared: forgiveness happens face to face.
neighbors.sources: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Repentance 2:10 (paraphrase) · Mishnah Yoma 8:9 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the whole earth is family
neighbors.text: Today a pope and a Grand Imam signed a page calling all people brothers and sisters. Hindus have an old line for that: vasudhaiva kutumbakam. In the Maha Upanishad it reads, roughly: small minds keep count, this one is mine, that one a stranger; for the large-hearted, the whole earth is one family.
neighbors.difference: Catholics call people brothers and sisters as children of one Father, each made by God. For many Hindus, the family rests on the same divine Self living in every being, so no one is truly a stranger.
neighbors.shared: no one on earth is truly a stranger.

neighbors.heading: that you may know one another
neighbors.text: Today a pope and the Grand Imam of al-Azhar signed a page calling all people brothers and sisters. Muslims hear that in the Qur'an: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Different peoples, the verse says, so that we meet.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, fraternity rests on one Father of all. The Qur'an speaks of one Creator, never called Father, and adds that the noblest in God's sight is the one best in conduct, whatever their people.
neighbors.shared: our differences are a reason to meet, not to fight.

neighbors.heading: a royal priesthood
neighbors.text: Today ordinary Catholics, not priests, started movements that fed the poor and worked for peace. Protestant Christians built a whole teaching on that. Martin Luther wrote that every baptized Christian belongs to the spiritual estate, a priest before God. They point to Peter's letter: "But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation".
neighbors.difference: Catholics teach that the baptized share in Christ's priesthood, and that ordained priests serve them in a different way, at the altar. Many Protestant churches see their pastors as believers called to a role, not set apart in a different kind of priesthood.
neighbors.shared: holiness isn't only for the people up front.
neighbors.sources: 1 Peter 2:9 (KJV) · Martin Luther, To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1547 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no priest at the front
neighbors.text: Today ordinary Catholics started movements that fed the poor and worked for peace. Sikhs have no priestly class at all. Any Sikh, woman or man, may read from the Guru Granth Sahib, lead the prayer or sing in the gurdwara. Guru Gobind Singh, tradition says, placed the Guru's authority in the scripture and in the gathered community, the Khalsa Panth.
neighbors.difference: Focolare and Sant'Egidio work alongside bishops and priests, whom Catholics keep for the sacraments. Sikhs have granthis who care for the scripture, but they serve the congregation, and anyone in it may take their place.
neighbors.shared: the people in the pews can lead too.
neighbors.sources: Sikh Rehat Maryada, on gurdwara services (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: thirty-six hidden ones
neighbors.text: Today the question was: are there saints now? The Talmud gives a Jewish answer. A rabbi named Abaye taught that the world never has fewer than thirty-six righteous people in each generation, who receive God's presence. Later Jewish folk tradition added a twist: they're hidden and humble, maybe a cobbler or a water carrier, and may not know it themselves.
neighbors.difference: The Church names some of its saints after careful study, with feast days and a calendar. The thirty-six are never named or declared; Jewish tradition keeps them unknown, and some say the world stands because of them.
neighbors.shared: goodness keeps showing up, often where no one's looking.

neighbors.heading: the world won't be empty
neighbors.text: Today the question was: are there saints now? Buddhists asked something like it. As the Buddha lay dying, a wandering seeker named Subhadda came with questions. The Buddha told him that as long as people truly walk the noble eightfold path, the world won't be empty of arahants, the awakened ones, freed from craving.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, holiness is God's gift, a life shared with Christ, and the saints in heaven pray for us. For Buddhists, awakening comes by walking the path the Buddha showed, with no creator granting it, and the arahant is freed from rebirth.
neighbors.shared: the people who live it fully aren't only in old books.
neighbors.sources: Digha Nikaya 16, Maha-parinibbana Sutta, the Subhadda episode (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the cave on the mountain
neighbors.text: Today Anthony left the village for the desert, alone with God. Muslims remember a retreat too. Before the Qur'an came to him, the Prophet Muhammad would go up to a cave on Mount Hira, outside Mecca, and spend nights there alone in worship. Then he came back down, to his wife Khadijah and his town.
neighbors.difference: Anthony stayed in the desert for years, and monks followed him. Islam has no monks; the Prophet's way was to retreat for a season and return to family and town. Many Muslims still keep a short retreat in the mosque in Ramadan's last nights.
neighbors.shared: sometimes you step away so you can hear clearly.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, the beginning of revelation (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: to the woods
neighbors.text: Today Anthony heard one line and walked out into the desert. Centuries later, an American writer tried his own version. Henry David Thoreau built a small cabin at Walden Pond and lived there plainly for a while. He explained why: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life".
neighbors.difference: Anthony gave everything away to follow Jesus and made the desert his home for life. Thoreau went to learn what life had to teach, on his own terms, with no vow, and came back to town after about two years.
neighbors.shared: less noise can make room for what matters.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden (1854), 'Where I Lived, and What I Lived For' (Thoreau)

items.lessonTitle: Francis de Sales, patron of writers (24 January)

neighbors.heading: holy at home
neighbors.text: Today Francis de Sales wrote for ordinary people: a holy life looks different for a soldier, a shopkeeper, a mother. Sikhs build their whole path that way. Guru Nanak turned away from leaving home for the forest. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan sings that, meeting the True Guru, you can be freed while laughing, playing, dressing and eating.
neighbors.difference: Francis also honored monks and nuns, and saw theirs as one holy calling among many. Sikh teaching sees the householder's life of work, family and service as the path itself, and most of the Gurus married and raised families.
neighbors.shared: the kitchen and the workplace can be holy ground.

neighbors.heading: your own work
neighbors.text: Today Francis de Sales wrote that devotion fits each life differently: a soldier's, a merchant's, a mother's. The Bhagavad Gita says something close. Arjuna wants to drop his duty and walk away. Krishna tells him to do the work that's truly his, without clinging to the results; better your own duty done imperfectly than another's done well.
neighbors.difference: For Francis, every life's devotion is love of God, shaped by its calling. In the Gita, dharma is the duty that belongs to a person's place and nature, and work done without clinging becomes a path to freedom.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to leave your life to find what's holy in it.

neighbors.heading: in your own dialect
neighbors.text: Today two brothers built an alphabet so Slavic peoples could hear the Gospel in their own speech. Buddhists remember the Buddha facing that question. Two monks asked to set his teaching into a grand old style of verse. He said no. Instead, the monastic rule says, he allowed his followers to learn his words in their own dialect, as many scholars read the line.
neighbors.difference: Cyril and Methodius translated words Catholics hold to be inspired by God, with the pope's approval. The Buddha's words are a teacher's guidance, not a god's revelation, and understanding them matters most. Many Theravada Buddhists still also chant in Pali.
neighbors.shared: a teaching should reach people in the words they dream in.

neighbors.heading: the boy behind the plough
neighbors.text: Today two brothers built an alphabet so Slavic peoples could hear the Gospel in their own tongue. English Protestants fought for the same thing. William Tyndale translated the New Testament into English, and is remembered for vowing that a boy behind the plough would know more Scripture than a learned cleric. He was executed as a heretic; his wording lives on in the King James Bible.
neighbors.difference: Cyril and Methodius won the pope's blessing for their Slavonic books. Tyndale worked without church approval, in exile. Protestants hold Scripture as the final authority, so every reader needs it; Catholics read it within the Church's living tradition.
neighbors.shared: God's word, heard in the language of home.
neighbors.sources: John Foxe, Acts and Monuments, on William Tyndale (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: it's not too late
neighbors.text: Today a dying thief asked for very little and was promised paradise. Tolstoy wrote a story about a late turn. Ivan Ilyich, a judge who lived for comfort and approval, lies dying and in pain. In his last hours he feels pity for his wife and son, tries to ask their forgiveness, and finds that in place of death there is light.
neighbors.difference: Dismas's hope rests on Jesus, and a promise of paradise that same day. Tolstoy leaves the meaning to the reader: Ivan finds peace in compassion and honesty at the end, and the story doesn't say what lies beyond.
neighbors.shared: one honest moment can change how a whole life ends.
neighbors.sources: Leo Tolstoy, The Death of Ivan Ilyich, ch. 12 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a world in one hour
neighbors.text: Today a dying thief asked to be remembered and was promised paradise. The Talmud tells of Elazar ben Durdaya, who had lived badly for years, then turned with his whole heart and died weeping. A heavenly voice said he was welcomed into the world to come. Rabbi Judah the Prince wept too: some gain their world in a single hour.
neighbors.difference: Dismas turns to Jesus beside him and receives a promise from him. In Jewish teaching, repentance turns straight to God, with no one in between, and wrongs done to people still have to be made right with them.
neighbors.shared: it's never too late to turn around.

neighbors.heading: work as an offering
neighbors.text: Today the Church set a carpenter's bench in the middle of the calendar: ordinary work is not time away from God. The Bhagavad Gita says it too. Krishna tells Arjuna: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give, do it as an offering to me. Work done that way, he says, no longer binds you.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, work is holy because Jesus, God made man, learned a trade beside Joseph. In the Gita, work becomes holy when it's offered to Krishna and done without clinging, and that frees a person from karma's binding.
neighbors.shared: a workbench can be an altar.

neighbors.heading: from the work of his hands
neighbors.text: Today the Church honored Joseph, a carpenter, and said ordinary work is holy. Muslims keep a saying of the Prophet Muhammad close to that: no one eats better food than what they earn with their own hands, and the prophet David ate from the work of his hands. At home, his wife Aisha said, the Prophet helped his family with their work.
neighbors.difference: The feast puts the honor of work inside a family: Jesus learning a trade from Joseph. The hadith ties it to honest earning: eating from your own hands rather than living off others or having to ask.
neighbors.shared: honest work with your hands is never small.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Sales, on earning by one's own hand (paraphrase) · Sahih al-Bukhari, on the Prophet serving his family (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: how sweet the name
neighbors.text: Today Bernardine held up three letters, IHS, and asked a crowd to honor the name of Jesus. Protestant Christians sing their love for that name. John Newton, the former slave-ship captain who wrote Amazing Grace, also wrote a hymn that begins: "How sweet the name of Jesus sounds / In a believer's ear!" Congregations still sing it.
neighbors.difference: Bernardine's board was a sign to look at and honor, and some critics in his own day worried about that. Many Protestants honor the Name in song, prayer and preaching, and keep their church walls plainer.
neighbors.shared: a name you love can steady you all day.
neighbors.sources: John Newton, Olney Hymns (1779), 'How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds' (public domain)

neighbors.heading: remembering the name
neighbors.text: Today Bernardine held up a name and asked a crowd to honor it. Sikhs build their day around a Name too. Naam japna, remembering God's Name, is one of three pillars Guru Nanak taught, with honest work and sharing. Sikhs repeat Waheguru, wonderful Lord, in prayer and under their breath, so the Name keeps them company.
neighbors.difference: Bernardine honored Jesus, God made man, whose name can be written in three letters. In the Mool Mantar, Sikhs speak of God as beyond birth and form, and Naam is more than a word: it is God's presence filling all things.
neighbors.shared: a name said with love keeps you company.
neighbors.sources: Mool Mantar, Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (paraphrase) · Sikh Rehat Maryada, on naam simran (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the mother bird
neighbors.text: Today Kevin held his hand still so a blackbird could raise her young. The Torah has a law about a nest too. If you find a bird's nest by the road, with the mother sitting on her eggs or chicks, you may not take the mother with the young; send her away first. Jewish law calls the pain of animals something to care about: tza'ar ba'alei chayim.
neighbors.difference: Kevin's stillness is a legend, told as a picture of patient prayer. The nest law is a commandment for daily life, and the rabbis debated its reason: some heard mercy for the mother, others a law kept simply because God commanded it.
neighbors.shared: a small creature can teach us to be gentle.

neighbors.heading: every creature trembles
neighbors.text: Today Kevin held still so a blackbird could trust him with her eggs. Buddhists start their practice with that kind of care. The first precept is to refrain from harming living things. The Dhammapada gives the reason: every creature trembles at harm and fears death, so put yourself in its place, and don't kill or cause killing.
neighbors.difference: In Kevin's story, the bird's trust shows a man at rest in God, and creation as God's gift. For Buddhists, animals are fellow beings in the round of rebirth, and not harming them is a training each person takes on.
neighbors.shared: every creature wants to live, and can feel your gentleness.

neighbors.heading: a traveler passing through
neighbors.text: Today a rich Roman gave his fortune away, slowly, and kept his pen for God. Muslims remember the Prophet Muhammad taking a young companion, Ibn Umar, by the shoulder and saying: be in this world as if you were a stranger, or a traveler passing through. The reports say the Prophet slept on a simple mat that left marks on his side.
neighbors.difference: Paulinus answered Jesus' call to sell what he had and give it to the poor. Islam doesn't ask believers to give everything away; it asks them to hold wealth lightly, pay zakat, give freely, and not let the world own them.
neighbors.shared: you can travel light and still give a lot.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Riqaq, the hadith of Ibn Umar (paraphrase) · Sahih al-Bukhari, the report of Umar on the Prophet's mat (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: who's really poor
neighbors.text: Today a rich Roman gave his fortune away and found he wasn't poorer. An earlier Roman philosopher, Seneca, wrote to a friend about the same discovery: "It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor." He even suggested a few days of plain food and rough clothes now and then, to lose the fear of having less.
neighbors.difference: Paulinus gave his wealth to the poor and the Church, for love of Christ. Seneca stayed a rich man; his aim was freedom from craving and fear, practiced in the mind, and his letters argue from reason, not from faith.
neighbors.shared: having enough begins with wanting less.
neighbors.sources: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 2 (Gummere) · Moral Letters 18 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: water for both sides
neighbors.text: Today Camillus gathered men to nurse the sick like a mother nurses her only child. Sikhs tell of Bhai Ghanaiya, who carried water to wounded soldiers on the battlefield, enemies included. When others complained to Guru Gobind Singh, he answered that he saw no enemy, only the Guru's light in every face. The Guru blessed him, and gave him ointment too.
neighbors.difference: Camillus served the sick in Christ's name, seeing Christ in each patient, as Matthew's Gospel teaches. Bhai Ghanaiya served as a Sikh layman, and the reason he gave was the one divine Light shining in friend and foe alike.
neighbors.shared: the person in pain is never the enemy.

neighbors.heading: serving god in people
neighbors.text: Today Camillus founded an order to nurse the sick the way a mother nurses her only child. A Hindu monk, Swami Vivekananda, built the Ramakrishna Mission on an idea his teacher Ramakrishna taught: don't just pity people, serve them as God. The mission still runs hospitals and relief work.
neighbors.difference: Camillus saw Christ in the sick, as Jesus says in Matthew's Gospel: you did it to me. For Vivekananda, following Vedanta, God is present as the very Self of every being, so serving a person is serving God directly.
neighbors.shared: caring for the sick is a way of meeting God.
neighbors.sources: Swami Vivekananda, Complete Works (paraphrase) · Ramakrishna's teaching on serving Shiva in every being (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the water in the dipper
neighbors.text: Today Jesus praised Nathanael as a man with nothing hidden. The Buddha taught his young son Rahula about honesty with a dipper of water. He left a little in it: that's how little is left of the practice of someone unashamed to lie on purpose. Then he tipped it out, and turned the dipper upside down, empty.
neighbors.difference: Jesus sees into Nathanael's heart and names his honesty as something good. For Buddhists, truthful speech is a training a person takes up, part of the eightfold path, because lies cloud the mind of the one who tells them.
neighbors.shared: a life with nothing hidden is lighter to carry.

neighbors.heading: let your yea be yea
neighbors.text: Today Jesus praised a man with no guile, nothing hidden. Quakers, the Religious Society of Friends, took honesty so seriously that they refused to swear oaths, even in court, which once cost them fines and prison. Their reason was a line of Jesus: "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay." If you always tell the truth, they said, an oath adds nothing.
neighbors.difference: Catholics read Jesus' words as allowing oaths for serious reasons, such as in court, taken with care. Quakers decline every oath, to show there's no second, lower standard of truth.
neighbors.shared: your plain word should be enough.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 5:37 (KJV) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2154 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: know the other side
neighbors.text: Today two bishops disagreed and stayed friends, and Cyprian worked his way closer to Cornelius. The philosopher John Stuart Mill argued that disagreement keeps us honest. In On Liberty he wrote: "He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that." Hearing the other side at its strongest, he said, is how we hold the truth as truth.
neighbors.difference: Cornelius and Cyprian argued inside one faith, aiming for the Church's unity in Christ. Mill trusted open debate among free people, with no final authority but reason and evidence, to bring the truth out over time.
neighbors.shared: a good friend can tell you you're wrong.
neighbors.sources: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (1859), ch. 2 (public domain)

neighbors.heading: these and these
neighbors.text: Today two bishops disagreed, kept writing as brothers, and are named side by side at Mass. The Talmud remembers two schools that argued for years, Hillel's and Shammai's. A heavenly voice said both were the words of the living God. The law followed Hillel, the rabbis said, because his students were kind and humble, and taught Shammai's view first.
neighbors.difference: Catholic disagreements are finally settled by the bishops together with the pope, and unity means staying in one communion. The Talmud also follows one side in practice, but keeps the other side's words on the page, still studied today.
neighbors.shared: you can disagree hard and still call each other friend.

neighbors.heading: give with faith
neighbors.text: Today Hedwig gave gladly, out of what she had, and Paul says God loves a cheerful giver. The Taittiriya Upanishad sends students home with advice about giving: give with faith, not without it; give generously; give with modesty; give with awe; give with understanding. The Bhagavad Gita adds that the purest gift is given at the right time, to the right person, expecting nothing back.
neighbors.difference: Hedwig gave as a Christian sharing in Christ's love for the poor, sometimes serving them at her own table. In Hindu teaching, dana, giving, is a duty and a discipline of its own, and the right spirit purifies the giver.
neighbors.shared: how you give matters as much as what you give.

neighbors.heading: no reward, no thanks
neighbors.text: Today Hedwig gave gladly, from what she had, and served the poor at her own table. The Qur'an describes the righteous feeding the needy, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of God, and saying: "We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you".
neighbors.difference: Hedwig gave far beyond what any rule asked, out of love for Christ in the poor. The Qur'an also says the poor have a known right in the wealth of the well-off, so giving is a duty as well as a gift.
neighbors.shared: a gift for God's sake asks nothing back.

neighbors.heading: two books
neighbors.text: Today Albert the Great studied leaves, stones and stars, sure that honest study of the world leads toward God. An English writer and statesman of the Church of England, Francis Bacon, put it as two books: God's word in Scripture and God's works in nature. No one, he wrote, can study either book too much, as long as they don't jumble the two together.
neighbors.difference: Albert, a friar, read nature inside the Church's teaching and alongside Aristotle. Bacon wanted the two books kept apart, each read by its own method, and helped shape science as its own careful way of testing.
neighbors.shared: looking closely at the world can be a kind of praise.
neighbors.sources: Francis Bacon, The Advancement of Learning, Book 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: worlds beyond worlds
neighbors.text: Today Albert the Great studied leaves, stones and stars, reading the world as God's work. Guru Nanak looked up too. In the Japji he sings of worlds below worlds and skies above skies, hundreds of thousands of them. People search for the edge and grow tired, he says. It's too great to write down; only the Creator knows how great.
neighbors.difference: Albert set out to observe and describe nature piece by piece, checking for himself. Guru Nanak's hymn is about awe: creation runs past every count, and the fitting answer is wonder and praise of the One who made it.
neighbors.shared: the more you look, the bigger the wonder gets.
neighbors.sources: Japji Sahib, pauri 22, Guru Granth Sahib (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a hundred blessings
neighbors.text: Today the Potawatomi named Philippine the woman who prays always. Jewish life weaves prayer through the whole day too. In the Talmud, Rabbi Meir teaches that a person should say a hundred blessings every day. There are blessings for waking, for bread, for thunder, for a rainbow, even for leaving the bathroom: thanks threaded through ordinary hours.
neighbors.difference: Philippine prayed long hours in a chapel, often in silence. Jewish blessings are short and tied to moments: a bite, a sound, a sight. Many say them in Hebrew, with set words, so the whole day gets marked, not just its quiet hours.
neighbors.shared: any moment of the day can turn into a prayer.

neighbors.heading: walking, standing, sitting
neighbors.text: Today the Potawatomi named Philippine the woman who prays always. Buddhists practice an awareness that runs all day too. In the Satipatthana Sutta, the Buddha teaches knowing, while walking, that you walk; while standing, that you stand; while sitting or lying down, the same. Eating, drinking, even dressing can be done with full attention.
neighbors.difference: Philippine's prayer was turned toward God, a conversation with someone she loved. Buddhist mindfulness doesn't address a god; it's attention to the present moment, training the mind to see clearly and let go of craving.
neighbors.shared: the whole day can be lived awake.

neighbors.heading: the left hand doesn't know
neighbors.text: Today Nicholas threw gold through a window at night and asked to be told by no one. Muslims know nearly the same picture. The Prophet Muhammad named seven people God shades on the Day when there is no shade but his; one gives charity so secretly that the left hand doesn't know what the right hand gave. The Qur'an says hidden alms are better.
neighbors.difference: Nicholas follows Jesus' words, where God is the Father who sees in secret. Islam never calls God Father; the reward is pictured as God's shade on the Day of Judgment, and the Qur'an also calls open giving good.
neighbors.shared: a gift is purest when only God sees it.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, the hadith of the seven given shade (paraphrase) · Qur'an 2:271 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: like a vine
neighbors.text: Today Nicholas threw gold through a window and asked the father to tell no one. Marcus Aurelius, a Roman emperor, described that kind of giving. Some people keep count of their favors, he wrote. Better to be like a vine that bears its grapes and asks nothing more, or a bee that has made its honey, and then simply goes on to the next good act.
neighbors.difference: Nicholas hid his gift because Jesus taught that the Father who sees in secret repays. Marcus expects no reward at all; doing good is simply what a person is made for, as fruit is for a vine.
neighbors.shared: the best kindness doesn't wait to be noticed.

neighbors.heading: the company of the holy
neighbors.text: Today Pope Francis's saints next door: the neighbor driving someone to chemo, the nurse on nights. Sikhs prize that kind of company. The Guru Granth Sahib praises the sadh sangat, the company of the holy, ordinary people gathered to remember God. In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan sings that in such company the face grows bright and the heart's dirt washes away.
neighbors.difference: Catholics use the word saint for all the baptized and, in a narrower sense, for those the Church declares in heaven. Sikhs speak instead of the gurmukh, the one turned toward the Guru, and of the sangat, where the Guru's presence is felt.
neighbors.shared: holy people are often the ones right beside you.
neighbors.sources: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtapadi 7, Guru Granth Sahib (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: dear to me
neighbors.text: Today Pope Francis's saints next door: holy people with no feast day, just steady love. The Bhagavad Gita describes such a person too. Krishna lists who is dear to him: someone who hates no creature, who is friendly and compassionate, free of 'mine' and pride, patient, the same in praise and blame, content with what comes.
neighbors.difference: Francis's saints are holy by sharing in God's grace through Christ, seen in ordinary love. In the Gita, these marks belong to the bhakta, the devotee whose heart rests in Krishna, and they ripen through devotion and practice.
neighbors.shared: holiness looks like quiet kindness, day after day.
